6910: Ghee is a type of pure, clarified fat made from butter — most commonly cow's butter — that has been slowly cooked until all its water has evaporated and all its milk solids have been removed. What remains is nearly 100% pure butterfat: a rich, golden, highly shelf-stable cooking fat.
The simplest way to picture it

Start with regular butter. Butter is not pure fat — it contains water (about 15–17%) and milk proteins and sugars (about 3–5%). When you melt butter in a pan on low heat and keep it going long enough, three things happen: the water boils away as steam, and the milk proteins and sugars sink to the bottom and gently toast or float to the top as foam. You skim or strain those solids away, and what you're left with — that clear, golden liquid — is ghee. It is butter, stripped down to its purest form.
What it looks, smells, and tastes like

• Color: Deep golden-yellow, sometimes amber. The longer it is cooked, the deeper the color.
  • Texture: At room temperature (below roughly 25°C / 77°F), ghee is semi-solid or fully solid, like soft wax or thick coconut oil. When warm, it is a clear, flowing liquid.
  • Smell: Distinctly nutty, warm, and rich — noticeably more flavorful than plain melted butter. This nutty aroma comes from the milk solids having gently browned before being removed, a process very similar to making "brown butter."
  • Taste: Deep, buttery, slightly caramel-like, and richer than ordinary butter. It coats the palate in a way that feels luxurious.
How ghee differs from regular butter and plain clarified butter

These three things are related but distinct:

Regular butter contains fat, water, and milk solids all together. Because of the water and proteins, it burns easily when heated, foams in the pan, and spoils relatively quickly.

Clarified butter is butter that has been melted and had its water and milk solids removed — similar to ghee, but the process stops earlier. It is cooked just long enough to separate the components, without letting the milk solids toast or brown at all.

Ghee goes one step further than clarified butter. It is cooked slowly and long enough that any remaining moisture is completely gone and the milk solids are allowed to brown slightly before being removed. This extra step is what gives ghee its distinctly deeper, nuttier flavor — and what makes it even more shelf-stable than clarified butter.

Think of it this way: clarified butter and ghee are made by the same method, but ghee is the more fully reduced, more flavorful, more traditional version of the two.
Where ghee comes from and its cultural importance

Ghee is deeply rooted in South Asian culture, particularly in India, where it has been made and used for thousands of years. It is a staple ingredient across Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Nepali, and Sri Lankan cooking. It also appears prominently in Middle Eastern and some Southeast Asian cuisines.

In India, ghee is not just food — it carries enormous cultural, religious, and symbolic significance. In Hinduism, it is considered sacred and pure. It is used in religious ceremonies, offered into sacred fires during rituals (havan or yagna), and used to light oil lamps in temples and homes. It is also a central ingredient in Ayurveda, the ancient Indian system of medicine, where it is regarded as deeply nourishing and healing — believed to aid digestion, strengthen the body, and support overall health.

In many South Asian households, homemade ghee — simmered slowly from cultured butter or cream — is a matter of household pride and tradition.
How ghee is used in cooking

Ghee is an extremely versatile cooking fat. Its most practical advantage over butter is its very high smoke point — around 250°C (480°F), compared to regular butter's 150°C (300°F). This means you can use ghee for high-heat cooking like deep-frying, sautéing, and searing without it burning or smoking, something butter simply cannot do.

Some common uses:

  • As a cooking fat for frying spices, onions, and aromatics at the start of curries and dals — the heat releases the flavor of the spices directly into the ghee, which then carries those flavors throughout the dish.
  • For making rice dishes like biryani and pulao, where ghee is mixed in for richness and flavor.
  • Drizzled over finished dishes — a small spoonful of ghee poured over hot dal (lentil soup), rice, khichdi, or roti just before eating adds enormous flavor and richness.
  • In baking and sweets — ghee is essential in Indian sweets (mithai) like halwa, ladoo, and mysore pak, giving them their characteristic richness.
  • Spread on flatbreads — rotis, parathas, and naans are often finished with a brush of ghee right off the heat.
  • As a finishing fat in many global cuisines, drizzled over vegetables, meats, or soups for flavor.

Because ghee has no water and no milk solids, it does not spoil the way butter does. It is highly resistant to bacterial growth and rancidity. Properly made ghee stored in a clean, dry, airtight container can last:

  • At room temperature: Several weeks to a few months.
  • In the refrigerator: Up to a year or more.
  • In the freezer: Indefinitely.

A critical rule: always use a dry spoon to scoop ghee. Even a small drop of water introduced into the jar can cause it to spoil much faster.

Ghee is almost entirely saturated fat, since it is pure butterfat. It contains fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E, and K — which are retained from the original butter. Because the milk solids (which contain lactose and casein, the milk sugar and milk protein) are removed during the making of ghee, people who are lactose intolerant or sensitive to dairy proteins often find they can tolerate ghee even when they cannot tolerate butter or other dairy products. However, it is important to note that ghee is a calorie-dense fat, and how much of it is healthy to consume depends entirely on the overall context of a person's diet.

Ghee is butter cooked down to its purest fat form — water gone, milk solids removed — leaving a golden, nutty, shelf-stable cooking fat with a deep flavor, a very high smoke point, and enormous cultural significance across South Asia. It is at once a practical kitchen staple, a sacred ritual ingredient, and a centuries-old symbol of nourishment and purity.
6911:
A ghetto is a section of a city — a specific neighborhood or district — where people from a particular group (defined by race, religion, or ethnicity) live together, separated from the rest of the city's population. The defining characteristic that makes a ghetto different from just any ordinary neighborhood is this: the people living there did not freely choose to be there. They were pushed there — either by law, by discrimination, by poverty, or by a combination of all three — and they typically have limited or no realistic way to leave.

Think of it as a city-within-a-city: a pocket of the urban area that is visibly poorer, more neglected, and more isolated than surrounding areas, and whose residents belong predominantly to a group that the wider society has, in some way, excluded.

The word carries two closely related but historically distinct meanings.

1. The Historical/Formal Meaning

In its oldest and most precise sense, a ghetto was a legally enforced zone inside a city where a specific minority group — most famously, Jewish people in Europe — was required by law to live. These were not neighborhoods people drifted into by circumstance. They were formally designated, sometimes physically walled off, and residents were often forbidden from leaving after dark or venturing into the rest of the city freely. Life inside was cramped, resources were scarce, and the people living there had no say in the matter.

The most extreme and devastating example of this in modern history was during World War II, when the Nazi regime created ghettos in cities across occupied Europe — such as the Warsaw Ghetto in Poland — where Jewish people were imprisoned in horrific conditions, often before being deported to concentration camps. These ghettos were not just poor neighborhoods; they were instruments of persecution and, ultimately, genocide.

This historical sense of the word is soaked in suffering. It describes forced segregation at its most brutal — the state using physical space to isolate, control, and dehumanize a group of people.

2. The Modern/Sociological Meaning

Today, the word is most commonly used to describe a poor, densely populated urban neighborhood that is home predominantly to a racial or ethnic minority group. In the United States — where the term gets a great deal of use — this has historically referred to inner-city neighborhoods primarily inhabited by Black Americans.

In this modern sense, there are no walls. There are no laws saying you must live there. And yet, the people in these neighborhoods are not there entirely by free choice either. They are there because of forces that are less visible but no less powerful than a locked gate:

Housing discrimination. For much of the 20th century in America, banks refused to give home loans to Black families in predominantly white neighborhoods — a practice called "redlining." Landlords refused to rent or sell to them. This funneled minority families into specific, limited parts of the city, regardless of their income or desires.

Poverty cycles. When a neighborhood becomes poor, it tends to stay poor and grow poorer. Businesses leave, tax revenues fall, schools deteriorate, infrastructure crumbles, and the job market dries up. Families who want to leave often cannot afford to. Poverty feeds on itself.

Systemic exclusion. Discrimination in hiring, in wages, in education, and in access to social services means that residents are perpetually disadvantaged in their ability to accumulate the wealth they would need to move.

The result is a neighborhood that looks and feels distinctly different from wealthier parts of the same city: run-down housing, potholed streets, underfunded and overcrowded schools, few grocery stores or hospitals nearby, and higher rates of crime — crime being largely a product of poverty, unemployment, and desperation, not of the character of the people living there.
What Makes a Ghetto Different from Just a "Poor Neighborhood"

This distinction matters. Not every poor area qualifies as a ghetto. Two things must work together:

First, the residents must belong predominantly to a specific minority group — the neighborhood is defined by ethnic, racial, or religious concentration, not just by economic class alone.

Second, there must be an element of involuntary confinement — either by explicit law (historically) or by the invisible but real walls of discrimination and poverty (in modern usage). People are not simply choosing to cluster there. They are there because they feel — correctly — that they have no realistic alternative.

A poor rural town would not be called a ghetto. A diverse low-income urban area might not qualify either. The word specifically names the intersection of minority identity and involuntary urban segregation.

Whether historical or modern, ghettos tend to share certain conditions. These are not accidental. They are the consequences of being a community that society has chosen to neglect:

Overcrowding. Many families packed into small, poorly maintained buildings. Landlords have little incentive to improve properties when tenants have nowhere else to go.

Poverty. Residents earn low wages, have limited job opportunities nearby, and struggle to save money or build wealth across generations.

Failing schools. Schools are often funded by local property taxes — which means that poor areas have poorly funded schools. Children grow up without access to quality education, making it harder to escape poverty. The cycle repeats.

Crumbling infrastructure. Streets, public transport, parks, and sanitation are neglected by city governments that invest more in wealthier areas.

Lack of basic services. Hospitals may be far away. Pharmacies and even grocery stores with fresh food may be scarce, creating what are sometimes called "food deserts."

Higher crime rates. This is perhaps the most misunderstood aspect of ghettos. High crime in these areas is not evidence of some inherent quality of the people who live there — it is a predictable outcome of poverty, unemployment, inadequate social services, and the presence of illegal economies that fill the gap left by legitimate ones.

Social isolation. The ghetto exists as a kind of separate world, cut off from the economic opportunity, cultural life, and social networks of the broader city. Residents often experience a kind of invisibility — present in the city but not fully part of it.
The Emotional and Moral Weight of the Word

"Ghetto" is not a neutral, descriptive word the way "suburb" or "downtown" is. It carries deep moral weight. To call a neighborhood a ghetto is to make an implicit statement about justice — or the lack of it. It implies that the people who live there were put there, that forces beyond their control shaped their circumstances, and that the conditions they face reflect a failure of the broader society, not of the individuals themselves.

When the word is used carelessly — or used to dismiss, mock, or belittle a community — it can be deeply dehumanizing. It reduces complex human lives and communities to a single label of poverty and dysfunction, erasing the dignity, resilience, and rich social fabric that exists within those communities.

Many people who grew up in or come from such neighborhoods have complicated feelings about the word. Some reclaim it as part of their identity — a badge of survival and pride. Others reject it as a stigma imposed by outsiders who see only the deprivation and none of the humanity.
The Informal Slang Use — and Why It Is Offensive

It is worth briefly knowing that "ghetto" has also been used informally in everyday speech as an adjective — to describe something as cheap, makeshift, low-quality, or unsophisticated. For example: "That repair job looks so ghetto" meaning it looks shoddy or thrown together.

This informal use is widely considered offensive. The reason is straightforward: it takes a word associated with communities that are predominantly poor and belong to racial minorities — communities that face real injustice — and uses it as a synonym for "bad," "inferior," or "tacky." This implicitly suggests that the people associated with those communities are themselves lesser. Most thoughtful speakers avoid this usage entirely.

The word "ghetto" names something that happens when a society treats a particular group of people as unworthy of equal participation in civic life. Whether you are reading about walled Jewish quarters in medieval European cities, Nazi-created prison zones during World War II, or the segregated inner-city neighborhoods that formed in 20th-century America, the same underlying story is present: a group of people confined, by power and prejudice, to a life apart.

To understand the word fully is to understand not just what a ghetto looks like — the cracked streets, the overcrowded apartments, the struggling schools — but why it exists. And the answer to that "why" is always the same: it exists because some people were given power over others, and they used that power to exclude.

The word, used carefully and honestly, is not just a description of a place. It is a diagnosis of a society's failures.
6912:
To ghettoize means to separate, isolate, or push a group of people — or even a type of idea, art, or culture — into a confined space, a lower category, or a marginalized position, usually in a way that is unfair and harmful to their opportunities and standing in society.

The people or things being ghettoized end up cut off from the wider world — from resources, mainstream society, or equal treatment. They are treated as if they don't belong in the "main" space, so they get pushed into a separate, lesser one.
The literal meaning: people and physical places

In its most direct sense, to ghettoize a group of people means to force them — through official policies, laws, social discrimination, or economic pressure — to live in a specific, often neglected, area of a city, separated from the rest of society.

This usually happens to racial, ethnic, or religious minorities, or to very poor communities. The group doesn't freely choose to be there. They are pushed there — either by outright force, or because discrimination shuts every other door on them.

"Decades of discriminatory housing policies ghettoized Black families in the most neglected parts of the city."

This sentence means: Those policies forced Black families into specific, underserved neighborhoods and prevented them from living elsewhere.
The figurative meaning: ideas, art, culture, and professions

This is where the word becomes especially interesting — and it's actually where you'll encounter it most often in modern writing.

"Ghettoize" doesn't only apply to physical spaces and communities. It can also describe the act of pushing anything — a genre of art, a group's concerns, a type of profession, a field of knowledge — into a corner where it is treated as less important, less serious, or less worthy of mainstream attention.

When something is ghettoized in this way, it isn't physically locked away — but it is treated as though it doesn't belong in the "main" conversation. It gets quietly sidelined.

"Science fiction was long ghettoized as low-brow entertainment, excluded from serious literary discussions."

This means: Serious literary critics refused to treat science fiction as real literature. They pushed it into a separate, lower-status category and didn't engage with it on equal terms.

"The company ghettoized its female employees by channeling them only into administrative roles, keeping them away from leadership tracks."

This means: The company quietly confined women to a lesser category of work, cutting them off from the same opportunities their male colleagues had access to.
The key idea running through every use of this word

Whether used literally or figuratively, the core idea is always the same:

Someone with power takes a group of people — or a type of thing — and separates it from the mainstream, pushing it into a confined, lower-status space in a way that is unfair, limiting, and harmful to that group's dignity, standing, and future.

The word almost always carries a strong negative charge. When you say something "has been ghettoized," you are criticizing the people or systems that caused this separation. You are saying: this isolation is wrong. It is the result of prejudice or deliberate neglect — not a neutral or natural arrangement.
Who does it, and who is it done to?

This is an important nuance. Ghettoizing is always done by someone with more power — a government, a corporation, an institution, a cultural establishment, a social majority. And it is always done to those with less power — a minority group, a marginalized community, or something considered "outside the mainstream."

This means ghettoize is never a neutral word. It places moral blame squarely on the people or systems doing the separating.

You'll see the word used both ways, and both are common:

  • Active: "The city council ghettoized the immigrant community through zoning laws." (Someone is actively doing it.)
  • Passive: "The immigrant community was ghettoized over several decades." (It happened to them — often without naming who is responsible, but the criticism is still present.)

You'll also encounter closely related word forms: ghettoized as an adjective ("a ghettoized minority," "ghettoized music genres") and ghettoization as the noun form ("the ghettoization of low-income neighborhoods").

To ghettoize = to isolate and push someone or something into a confined, lesser space — whether physically or socially — in a way that is discriminatory and damaging to their standing and life chances. The agent doing this is always someone in a position of power. The word always carries criticism. It names not just a situation, but an injustice.
6913:
A ghost is the spirit or soul of a dead person that is believed to have remained in the world of the living instead of moving on after death.

Think of it this way: most people believe that when a person dies, their body stops working, but some traditions hold that a part of them — their spirit, their essence, their "inner self" — continues to exist. When that spirit lingers on Earth and can sometimes be seen, heard, or felt by the living, it is called a ghost.
What a Ghost Is Believed to Look Like and Do

Ghosts are traditionally described as:

  • Transparent or semi-visible — you can partially see through them, like a shadow with a shape
  • Pale or white — often glowing faintly or colorless
  • Silent — they drift or float rather than walk normally
  • Tied to a specific place — they tend to stay near the location where they lived, died, or had a strong emotional connection, such as a house, a room, or a graveyard

A place where a ghost is believed to live or appear repeatedly is called haunted, and the ghost is said to haunt that place. The ghost may appear at certain times, make sounds (footsteps, cries, knocking), move objects, or simply make the space feel cold and eerie.
Why Do Ghosts Exist? (The Belief Behind the Word)

In folklore and many cultural traditions, a ghost is thought to exist for a reason — it is a soul that has not found peace. Common reasons include:

  • The person died suddenly or violently and their spirit is confused
  • They left behind unfinished business in the living world
  • They are deeply attached to someone or something and cannot let go
  • They were wronged and seek justice or revenge

Because of this, ghosts are often associated with sadness, suffering, fear, and the unresolved past.
The Important Distinction: Ghost vs. Soul

Not every dead person becomes a ghost. A ghost specifically refers to the spirit of a dead person that has stayed behind in the visible world and can interact with or be perceived by living people. The broader idea of a spirit or soul that has passed on to another realm (heaven, the afterlife, etc.) is simply called a soul or spirit — not a ghost.

The word "ghost" is used beyond its supernatural meaning. These figurative uses all carry the same idea: something faint, barely-there, or left behind from something that no longer fully exists.

A ghost of something means a faint trace or a barely-noticeable amount of it:

  • "There wasn't a ghost of a chance he would win." — meaning absolutely no chance at all
  • "A ghost of a smile crossed her face." — meaning the tiniest, barely-visible hint of a smile

Ghost town — a town or city that was once full of life and people but is now empty and abandoned. The "ghost" here suggests the lingering emptiness of something that used to exist.

Ghostwriter (or ghost) — a person who secretly writes something (a book, speech, article) on behalf of another person, who then publishes it under their own name. The writer stays invisible, like a ghost. The short form "ghost" is used when referring to this person in publishing circles.

Ghost (in technology) — in computing and digital contexts, a "ghost" can refer to a duplicate image, a faint echo of an image on a screen, a hidden or deleted account that still leaves traces in a system, or a complete backup copy of a computer's hard drive (called a "disk ghost" or "ghost image").

Holy Ghost — in Christianity, this is the third person of the Holy Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Ghost/Holy Spirit). Here, "ghost" is an older word for "spirit," and it refers to the divine presence of God experienced in the world. This is a fixed religious phrase and not used in any other context.

PhraseWhat It Means

"You look like you've seen a ghost" — said to someone who appears suddenly pale, shocked, or terrified, as if they just witnessed something frightening.

"Give up the ghost" — to die, or for something (like a machine) to stop working permanently. The "ghost" here is the soul leaving the body.

"The ghost of someone/something" — a reminder or echo of someone or something from the past, e.g., "She is the ghost of her former self" means she has changed so much she barely resembles who she used to be.
Is a Ghost the Same as Other Supernatural Beings?

No. These are often confused, so it helps to know the difference:

  • A ghost is specifically the spirit of a dead human being.
  • A spirit is a broader term — it can be a ghost, but also a non-human supernatural being, or simply the soul of any living or dead thing.
  • A demon is an evil supernatural being, typically not the spirit of a dead person, but a separate kind of entity altogether.
  • A poltergeist (from German, meaning "noisy ghost") is a specific type of ghost known not for appearing visibly, but for making loud noises and throwing or moving objects. It is a ghost, but a particularly disruptive kind.
  • An apparition is the moment a ghost is seen or perceived — it is not a different kind of being, just the word for the visible appearance of a ghost.
  • A specter or spectre is simply another word for a ghost, slightly more formal or literary.
  • A phantom is also a near-synonym for ghost, though it can sometimes refer to something that is an illusion or does not truly exist.
  • A wraith is a ghost-like figure, often described as a dark or shadowy spirit, sometimes specifically the image of a person seen just before or just after their death.

Ghost means the spirit of a dead person lingering in the world of the living. It carries a sense of something invisible yet present, something from the past that refuses to disappear, something between worlds. Whether used literally (a haunting spirit), figuratively (a ghost of a chance), or in fixed phrases (the Holy Ghost, a ghostwriter), the word always holds onto that central feeling — the faint, mysterious presence of something that should no longer be there, but is.
6914: To ghostwrite something means to write it on behalf of another person, who then presents it to the world as if they wrote it themselves. You, the writer, stay completely invisible — like a ghost. You do all the writing work, but you get none of the public credit. The other person gets all of it.

Imagine your friend is a famous chef. She wants to publish a book about her life and her cooking secrets. The problem? She's brilliant in the kitchen, but she struggles to put words together on paper. So she hires you — a talented writer — to write the entire book for her. You interview her, listen to her stories, understand her voice and personality, and then you write every single sentence of that book. When the book is published, her name is on the cover. Not yours. She goes on TV to talk about "her book." People congratulate her. You, the actual writer, are never mentioned. You ghostwrote the book.
The Key Elements That Make It "Ghostwriting"

For something to count as ghostwriting, three things must be true simultaneously:

1. Someone else does the writing. The ghostwriter produces the actual words, sentences, paragraphs, and ideas — or shapes and organises the credited person's rough ideas into polished, readable writing.

2. The credited person takes ownership. The person who hired the ghostwriter presents the finished work publicly under their own name, as though they personally wrote every word.

3. The ghostwriter remains hidden. This is the soul of the concept. The ghostwriter's involvement is typically kept secret, either by mutual agreement or by a formal legal contract. The "ghost" in the word is a metaphor — the ghostwriter is present in the work (you can feel their craft) but invisible to the public (you cannot see them or know who they are).

People ghostwrite for others — and hire ghostwriters — for very practical, understandable reasons.

From the credited person's side, they may have fascinating knowledge, experiences, or ideas, but lack the writing skill, time, or patience to produce a polished piece of writing. A busy CEO might have powerful insights about business but no time to write a book. A celebrity might have a dramatic life story but cannot translate it into compelling prose. A politician might want speeches that sound eloquent and moving, but cannot craft such language themselves. They need someone who can write to do it for them.

From the ghostwriter's side, it is simply a job — and often a well-paying one. Professional ghostwriters are hired and paid (sometimes very generously) to lend their writing talent to someone else's project. They trade public credit for money. It is a deliberate, willing professional exchange.

Ghostwriting is far more common than most people realise, and it happens across many areas of life:

In books, especially memoirs, autobiographies, and self-help books. A huge proportion of celebrity books, business books, and even political memoirs are ghostwritten. The famous name on the cover drew you in — but a professional writer in the background actually wrote it.

In music, songwriters often ghostwrite lyrics for singers who then perform and release those songs as their own. This is extremely common in popular music.

In speeches, world leaders, executives, and public figures routinely deliver speeches that were written entirely by speechwriters — a form of ghostwriting.

In articles and blogs, busy professionals and public figures often hire ghostwriters to produce articles published under their name on websites, magazines, or social media.

In academic contexts, ghostwriting becomes ethically problematic and is generally considered cheating — if a student pays someone to write their essay and submits it as their own work, that is a form of ghostwriting that violates academic honesty rules.

In most professional and commercial contexts — books, music, business — ghostwriting is completely legal and widely accepted. There is no law against it. Society has largely normalised it because the exchange is consensual: the ghostwriter agrees to stay hidden, the credited person agrees to pay. Both parties get what they want.

However, ghostwriting sits in a morally grey zone for many people. There is a subtle dishonesty in presenting someone else's writing as your own. The reader who buys a celebrity's "autobiography" believes they are reading the celebrity's own words and thoughts — they don't know a professional writer shaped every sentence. Whether that matters ethically is something thoughtful people genuinely debate.

The clearest ethical violation occurs when ghostwriting is used to deceive in high-stakes situations — like academic fraud — where the whole purpose is to earn credit or qualifications you didn't actually earn.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The verb "ghostwrite" changes form depending on how you use it:

  • "She agreed to ghostwrite his memoir." (base/infinitive form)
  • "He ghostwrote three bestselling novels for that actress." (past tense — ghostwrote)
  • "The book was ghostwritten by a journalist in London." (past participle — ghostwritten)
  • "She has been ghostwriting speeches for politicians for twenty years." (present participle — ghostwriting)

Ghostwriter (noun) — the person who ghostwrites. "She hired a ghostwriter to write her business book."

Ghostwriting (noun/gerund) — the act or practice of ghostwriting. "Ghostwriting is a thriving industry."

Ghostwritten (adjective) — describes a work produced this way. "It was widely suspected to be a ghostwritten autobiography."

In one sentence: to ghostwrite is to write something for another person who will publicly claim it as their own work, while you, the real writer, remain completely anonymous and uncredited — like a ghost.
6915:
A ghostwriter is a person who is hired to write something for someone else, and who agrees to remain completely invisible — meaning the work is published or presented under the hiring person's name, not the ghostwriter's.

The person who hired the ghostwriter gets all the credit. The ghostwriter gets paid, stays silent, and is never officially mentioned. To the outside world, it looks like the hiring person wrote everything themselves.

Think about what a ghost is — something that exists and does real work, but cannot be seen. A ghostwriter is exactly that: a real person doing real writing, but one who deliberately disappears from the picture once the work is done. They leave no visible trace of their presence. This is where the name comes from — the writer is like a ghost: present in the work, but invisible to everyone.
What Exactly Does a Ghostwriter Do?

A ghostwriter's job is to capture and express someone else's ideas, voice, and story — but in writing, because that other person either cannot write well, does not have the time to write, or simply does not enjoy writing.

Here is how it typically works:

The ghostwriter spends a great deal of time with the client — reading their notes, listening to them speak, interviewing them, studying how they express themselves. The goal is to understand the client so deeply that when the ghostwriter sits down to write, the final piece sounds as if the client wrote every single word themselves. The tone, the personality, the opinions — all of it must match the client, not the ghostwriter.

This is what makes ghostwriting genuinely skilled and difficult work. The ghostwriter must essentially erase their own writing personality and wear someone else's like a costume.

Ghostwriters work across a remarkably wide range of content. The most well-known examples include:

Books and autobiographies — Many celebrities, politicians, athletes, and business leaders have published books "written by" themselves, when in reality a ghostwriter did the actual writing. The famous person provides the life story, the experiences, and the ideas. The ghostwriter shapes it all into a polished, readable book.

Speeches — World leaders, CEOs, and public figures routinely deliver speeches that were written entirely by ghostwriters. The people listening assume the speaker wrote the words themselves.

Songs and lyrics — In the music industry, ghostwriters frequently write songs for popular artists who then record and perform them as their own.

Articles and blog posts — Busy executives or public figures often publish articles under their own names that were written by ghostwriters hired behind the scenes.

Academic work — Though this is considered deeply unethical and is often against the rules, some people illegally hire ghostwriters to write essays and assignments for them.

The single most defining feature of a ghostwriter is the agreement to stay hidden. This is not an accident or an afterthought — it is the entire foundation of the arrangement. Before any writing begins, the ghostwriter and the client formally agree (usually in a legal contract) that:

  • The ghostwriter will not claim credit for the work.
  • The ghostwriter will not reveal that they wrote it.
  • The client's name will appear as the sole author.

This agreement is called a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) or a confidentiality clause. If a ghostwriter breaks this agreement and tells the world they wrote the work, the client can take legal action against them.

There are several completely reasonable and legitimate reasons:

Lack of writing skill — A person might have a brilliant, fascinating life story or a genuinely valuable idea, but simply lack the skill to write it in an engaging, publishable way. A ghostwriter bridges that gap.

Lack of time — Writing a full book can take years. A busy CEO, politician, or celebrity may simply not have that kind of time available.

Consistency and volume — Some public figures need to publish content regularly (articles, posts, speeches) and cannot keep up with the demand on their own.

They want the result, not the process — Some people are simply not interested in writing. They care about having a book or a speech that represents them well — they do not care about the act of writing it themselves.

This is one of the most common and interesting questions people have, and the answer is nuanced.

In most areas of life, ghostwriting is completely legal, widely accepted, and not considered dishonest at all. It has existed for centuries and is treated as a normal professional service, much like hiring a lawyer to write your legal documents or hiring an architect to design your house. You still own the house. No one expects you to have designed it yourself.

The publishing world, the music industry, the corporate world, and the political world all operate with the quiet, widespread understanding that ghostwriting happens constantly.

However, there are specific contexts where ghostwriting is considered dishonest and even forbidden — most notably in academic settings. When a student submits work for a grade, there is a clear expectation that they personally did the work. Hiring someone to write your essay and submitting it as your own violates the rules of academic integrity and is considered cheating.

So the ethics of ghostwriting depend heavily on context and expectation. In professional publishing, the expectation does not exist that a famous person wrote every word themselves. In a classroom, that expectation absolutely does exist.
A Simple Example to Tie It All Together

Imagine a retired football star named Marcus. He had an incredible career and a dramatic personal life. He wants to publish a memoir. The problem? Marcus hates writing and is not very good at it.

Marcus hires a ghostwriter — a talented professional writer named Sarah. Marcus spends weeks telling Sarah his stories, his feelings, and his memories. Sarah takes all of that and transforms it into a beautifully written, 300-page book. The book is published with the title: My Story — by Marcus Johnson.

Sarah's name appears nowhere on the cover, inside the book, or in any marketing material. She received a fee for her work. The world believes Marcus wrote the book. Marcus is legally and professionally entitled to call it his own. Sarah knew this was the deal from the beginning.

That is a ghostwriter.

A ghostwriter is a hired, invisible author. They do the real work of writing. They get paid for it. And then they deliberately step out of the spotlight so that someone else can take full credit. The arrangement is built on a formal agreement of secrecy. It is a profession that is legal and respected in most contexts, and it exists because good ideas and good writing are two very different skills — and not everyone who has one also has the other.
6916: A ghoul is an evil, monstrous being — found in folklore, horror stories, and fantasy — that is most famous for one deeply disturbing habit: feeding on the dead. Think of it as a creature that lurks in dark, forgotten places like graveyards or ruins, and survives by consuming human corpses. That single image — a sinister being drawn to death and the dead — is at the heart of everything the word "ghoul" means.

The ghoul originally comes from ancient Arabian mythology, and this is its richest, most detailed form.

In those stories, a ghoul is a type of evil spirit or demon — not a dead person brought back to life, but a dark supernatural creature that has always existed in the shadows. Here is what makes the original ghoul so distinct and frightening:

It haunts lonely, desolate places. Ghouls do not live among people. They dwell in graveyards, ruins, abandoned deserts, and dark wastelands — anywhere remote, where death lingers and no one watches.

It eats the dead. A ghoul's primary food source is human corpses. It digs up graves or waits near burial grounds to feed. This is the single most defining trait of a ghoul across all cultures and time periods.

It sometimes hunts the living. While corpses are its preference, a ghoul is not above attacking living humans, particularly lone travelers who stray into its territory. In some tales, it lures victims by disguising itself, then kills and eats them.

It can shapeshift. This is one of the ghoul's most terrifying powers. A ghoul can take on the appearance of the person it last consumed, tricking that person's family or friends into trusting it. It can also sometimes appear as an animal, most often a hyena, which itself is an animal historically associated with feeding on the dead.

It is cunning, not mindless. Unlike a brainless monster, the folklore ghoul is deceptive and intelligent — it plans, it lures, it disguises itself. That makes it more dangerous, not less.
The Modern Ghoul: Horror and Fantasy

As the word traveled into English horror literature, films, and fantasy games, the ghoul evolved but kept its essential DNA. In modern usage, a ghoul is typically portrayed as:

  • A corpse-like, undead humanoid creature — gaunt, pale, with sunken eyes and a decaying appearance.
  • A being that haunts graveyards and crypts and feeds on buried bodies.
  • A creature that is stronger and faster than a normal human, but soulless and driven purely by hunger.
  • Somewhere between a zombie and a demon in most fantasy systems — it has the rotting appearance of the undead but the predatory intelligence of a demon.

In horror fiction, encountering a ghoul almost always involves a graveyard at night, something being wrong with a burial site, or a creature that looks almost human but is deeply, wrongly off in some way.

In role-playing games and fantasy fiction, ghouls are often classified as a category of the undead — creatures that were once human but have been transformed into flesh-eating monsters, sometimes by a curse, dark magic, or even by eating human flesh themselves.

Here is where the word steps out of mythology and into real life. In everyday English, you can call a living, breathing person a ghoul — and it is a strong insult.

A ghoul in this sense is someone who takes a morbid, unhealthy pleasure in death, disaster, or suffering. It describes a person who seems to enjoy things that a normal, decent person would find horrifying or deeply upsetting.

Examples of ghoulish behavior in real life:

  • Someone who slows their car down at a terrible accident not out of concern, but just to stare at the wreckage and carnage.
  • A person who obsessively follows stories of murders, tragedies, or disasters with what feels like enjoyment rather than sympathy.
  • Someone who shows up at a funeral and seems almost excited by the grief and death around them.

The key idea here is not just interest in dark things — that is normal human curiosity. The word "ghoul" implies something colder: a delight in it, a feeding on it emotionally, in the same way the creature feeds on corpses. The metaphor is deliberate and powerful.
How a Ghoul Differs From Similar Creatures

Since ghouls often appear alongside other monsters, it helps to understand the distinctions:

Ghoul vs. Zombie: A zombie is typically a mindless, reanimated corpse. A ghoul is either a demon that was never human, or a transformed being that retains some cunning. Zombies shuffle; ghouls hunt.

Ghoul vs. Vampire: A vampire is elegant, seductive, and feeds on blood from the living. A ghoul is grotesque and feeds on flesh, preferably from the dead. Vampires crave living victims; ghouls are drawn to corpses.

Ghoul vs. Demon: A demon is a broad category of evil supernatural being with many possible forms and goals. A ghoul is a specific type with a specific hunger — it is a demon defined almost entirely by its relationship with death and corpses.

If you had to capture everything in one sentence: A ghoul is an evil, corpse-eating monster from folklore — cunning, often found in graveyards, sometimes able to disguise itself — and in everyday language, the word describes any person who takes a disturbing, indecent pleasure in death or human suffering.
6917:
To understand "ghoulish," you first need to know what a ghoul is. A ghoul is a creature from horror and folklore — an evil, monstrous being that feeds on dead human bodies and haunts graveyards. It is associated with death, corpses, and darkness.

Ghoulish simply means "like a ghoul" — anything that reminds you of that creature, or feels connected to it in some way. Think of it as a stamp you put on something to say: "This belongs to the dark, disturbing world of death and horror."
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. To describe something that looks or feels horrifying and morbid

When a thing, a scene, or an event is deeply disturbing, gruesome, or connected to death in a creepy way, you call it ghoulish.

  • The aftermath of the accident was ghoulish — it was not something any normal person would want to see.
  • The haunted house had ghoulish decorations: skulls, rotting flesh, and coffins everywhere.
  • The killer left behind a ghoulish scene that shocked even the most experienced detectives.

In this sense, "ghoulish" is stronger and more specific than just "scary" or "disturbing." It points directly at something that feels like it belongs in the dark world of death, decay, and horror.

2. To describe a person's attitude, interest, or behavior toward dark or morbid things

When a person is strangely fascinated or excited by things that most people find horrifying — like death, disasters, suffering, or gruesome events — their attitude is called ghoulish.

  • He had a ghoulish curiosity about how people die. He constantly read about murders and autopsies with excitement.
  • Some people gathered around the accident scene with ghoulish interest, trying to get a good look instead of turning away.
  • She laughed at the news of the tragedy, which everyone found ghoulish and deeply unsettling.

Here, ghoulish doesn't mean the person is literally a monster. It means their enjoyment or fascination is so focused on dark, morbid things that it feels unnatural and wrong — like something a ghoul would enjoy, not a normal human.

"Ghoulish" is always negative. It is never a compliment.

When you call something or someone ghoulish, you are signaling one or both of these things:

  • It is deeply disturbing — it belongs to the world of death and horror in a way that makes people uncomfortable.
  • It feels morally off — there is something wrong or unnatural about it. A normal, decent person would not enjoy this, would not laugh at this, and would not be drawn to this.

The word carries a sense of creepiness on top of darkness. It is not just "scary." It is eerie, unsettling, and associated with things most people feel they should look away from.
Ghoulish Humor and a Broader Use

One common phrase you will encounter is ghoulish humor (also called dark or morbid humor). This is when someone makes jokes about death, tragedy, suffering, or disaster. It is the kind of humor that makes some people laugh nervously and others feel uncomfortable.

  • The comedian's jokes about funerals and corpses were ghoulish, but strangely funny to some in the audience.

Over time, "ghoulish" has also expanded slightly to describe anything that is deeply unsettling or macabre, even outside a strict horror context:

  • The politician made a ghoulish proposal — it was shocking, cold, and showed complete disregard for human life.

Here, the speaker uses "ghoulish" to say: "This is so cold and disturbing that it doesn't feel human."
How It Compares to Similar Words

WordWhat It Emphasizes

Scary simply means something causes fear. Creepy means something causes a slow, uneasy discomfort. Gruesome focuses specifically on something being physically disgusting and bloody. Macabre means something is disturbing because it deals with death — this is the closest word to ghoulish.

Ghoulish is unique because it does two things at once: it connects something directly to death and horror, and it adds the sense that there is something wrong about an attraction to it. When you say someone's interest in a topic is ghoulish, you are saying their fascination is not just dark — it is the kind of fascination that a monster would have, not a healthy human being.
A Quick Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture a pale, hollow-eyed creature crouching in a graveyard at night, grinning over a dug-up coffin — completely at home in the world of death, decay, and horror.

Anything that reminds you of that image — whether it is a scene, a person's behavior, a laugh, a curiosity, or a piece of humor — can be called ghoulish.
6918:
To gibber means to speak very fast in a way that is impossible — or nearly impossible — to understand. The sounds coming out of someone's mouth when they gibber are jumbled, confused, and senseless. It is not simply speaking quietly or mumbling. It is speaking in a way that has lost its shape — words tumbling out in a disordered rush, stripped of any clear meaning.

Think of someone who has just seen something terrifying. Their mouth opens, sounds come out fast, but none of it makes sense. That is gibbering.

This word carries more than just the idea of "speaking unclearly." It always implies that something has overwhelmed the speaker's mind, causing their speech to break down. You do not gibber by accident or out of laziness. You gibber because an extreme emotion or mental state has seized control of you and your ability to speak normally has collapsed.

The most common causes of gibbering are:

  • Terror or panic — "She was gibbering with fear after hearing the noise downstairs."
  • Shock — "After the accident, he sat gibbering on the pavement, unable to say anything sensible."
  • Madness or mental breakdown — "The old man was found gibbering in the corner, speaking to people who weren't there."
  • Extreme excitement or hysteria — "The children were almost gibbering with excitement on Christmas morning."

Notice that in every case, the person has been pushed to a mental or emotional extreme. Their speech is a symptom of that extreme state, not a choice.

When someone gibbers, the output is not silence and not normal speech — it is something in between and broken. It might sound like:

  • Rapid, breathless half-words
  • Fragments of sentences that don't connect
  • Meaningless sounds mixed with actual words
  • Repetitive babbling

The listener cannot follow it. There is no thread to grab onto. This is what separates gibbering from, say, rambling (which is long and wandering but still followable) or mumbling (which is unclear in volume, not in sense).
It Can Also Apply to Animals

Gibber is sometimes used to describe the sounds made by animals — particularly monkeys and apes — who chatter and screech in a fast, seemingly senseless way. This usage reinforces the idea that gibbering is speech-like noise without meaning. When people are described as gibbering, this comparison is hovering in the background — the suggestion that their speech has become as uncontrolled as an animal's.
The Word Has a Slightly Unkind Edge

When you say someone is gibbering, you are not being fully neutral. The word has a faint quality of mockery or pity to it. Calling someone a "gibbering wreck" or "gibbering fool" is belittling — you are pointing out that they have lost control so completely that they cannot even speak properly. Even when it is not meant cruelly, the word highlights weakness, helplessness, or irrationality.

This means you should be thoughtful about when you use it to describe a real person, since it can sound dismissive. In creative writing or describing a fictional character, however, it is vivid and powerful.

Certain phrases with "gibber" appear again and again in English, and knowing them will help you recognise and use the word naturally:

  • "Gibbering wreck" — A person so frightened or distressed that they are completely falling apart. "By the end of the horror film, he was a gibbering wreck."
  • "Gibbering with fear/terror" — The most classic use. "She came running out of the haunted house, gibbering with terror."
  • "Gibbering idiot/fool" — A contemptuous phrase for someone behaving irrationally and incoherently. (Can be used affectionately in informal speech.)
  • "Gibbering away" — Talking continuously in a senseless, unstoppable way. "He was gibbering away to himself in the waiting room."
A Related Word You Should Know: Gibberish

The noun gibberish is a close cousin of gibber. Gibberish means language or speech that is completely meaningless and impossible to understand — the product of gibbering, so to speak. If someone gibbers, what comes out of their mouth is gibberish. The two words share the same family, and knowing one sharpens your understanding of the other.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Nearby WordHow It Differs from Gibber
  • Babble — Also means to talk in a confused, unclear way, but babble is softer and less extreme. A baby babbles. A brook babbles. Babbling can even sound pleasant. Gibbering never does — it always carries urgency, panic, or disorder.
  • Ramble — To talk at length and wander off the point, but rambling is still intelligible. A rambling person can be followed, just with effort. A gibbering person cannot be followed at all.
  • Mutter — To speak quietly and indistinctly, usually to oneself. Muttering is about low volume; gibbering is about incoherence and speed.
  • Rant — To speak loudly and passionately, often in anger. A rant has a clear emotional point, even if excessive. Gibbering has no clear point at all.

If you want to lock the word in your memory, hold this image: a person so frightened they have lost the ability to speak sensibly — mouth moving fast, eyes wide, sounds pouring out, but nothing making sense. That person is gibbering. The word captures not just the sound, but the reason behind it — a mind overwhelmed, speech broken, control gone.
6919: Gibberish is language — or something that pretends to be language — that makes no sense to the person hearing or reading it. It fails at the one job language has: communicating a clear meaning. When something is gibberish, your brain receives sounds or words, but cannot extract any understandable message from them. It's the verbal or written equivalent of noise.

There are a few different ways something can qualify as gibberish, and it's important to understand all of them.

1. Completely made-up sounds with no meaning at all.
This is the most basic form. Think of a toddler "talking" — they produce sounds that feel like speech, have a rhythm like speech, but carry zero meaning. An adult doing the same thing (making mouth-sounds that aren't real words) is also producing gibberish. Example: "Blabba wocka flim norp." That is pure gibberish — sounds that look like words on paper, but mean absolutely nothing.

2. Real words arranged in a way that makes no sense.
Sometimes you use actual, real words, but combine them so chaotically that no coherent thought comes through. Example: "The purple Tuesday sleeps loudly under a careful dog." Every single word there is a real English word, but together, they communicate nothing sensible. That is gibberish.

3. Language so technical, complex, or full of jargon that an ordinary person cannot understand it.
This is a slightly softer, more everyday use of the word. If a doctor rattles off a wall of medical terminology to a patient who has no medical knowledge, the patient might say, "I'm sorry, that was all gibberish to me." They don't literally mean the doctor spoke nonsense — they mean the language was so far beyond their understanding that it felt like meaningless noise. This usage is very common in everyday conversation.

4. Garbled, corrupted, or scrambled text/speech.
When something goes wrong during transmission or translation, clear language can turn into gibberish. If you have ever received a text message that looked like "Â£â€˜Ã§Å¾Ã¼Ã±" due to an encoding error, that's gibberish — it was probably real words at some point, but the scrambling destroyed all meaning. Similarly, if someone is speaking on a badly broken phone line and all you hear is fragmented static — "I need you to…zzz…the thing…kshhhh…tomorrow" — that garbled result is gibberish.

No matter which form it takes, all gibberish shares one defining quality: it fails to deliver an understandable meaning. The communication breaks down completely. Understanding is impossible, or so difficult that it practically amounts to impossible.

This is a small but useful grammar point. "Gibberish" is an uncountable noun (also called a mass noun), just like "water" or "sand." This means:

  • You do not say: "He spoke a gibberish." ❌
  • You do not say: "There were three gibberishes in his speech." ❌
  • You do say: "He spoke gibberish." ✅
  • You do say: "There was a lot of gibberish in his speech." ✅
  • You do say: "That was pure gibberish." ✅

Think of it the way you'd use "nonsense" — you wouldn't say "a nonsense" either.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Calling something "gibberish" is almost always a negative, dismissive judgment. It signals frustration, confusion, or contempt. When someone says "Stop talking gibberish!" they are not being polite — they're expressing that what was said was useless and incomprehensible.

It can also sometimes be used more lightheartedly. If a friend is half-asleep and mumbling incoherently, you might laugh and say "You're speaking complete gibberish right now." Here it's less of an insult and more of an observation.

Gibberish is not always an accident. It can be:

  • Unintentional — A person is so panicked, drunk, or confused that they produce incoherent speech. A corrupted computer file displays scrambled characters. These are cases where gibberish happened by accident.
  • Intentional — Children sometimes invent "secret languages" that sound like gibberish to outsiders but follow an invented internal rule. Actors playing aliens in films speak invented gibberish to mimic the sound of language without actually saying anything. Comedians sometimes use rapid-fire fake speech to get a laugh. In all these cases, gibberish is deliberately created for a purpose.
How It Differs from Similar Words

A few words are close in meaning but not identical:

  • Nonsense is the broader term. Something can be nonsense because it's factually absurd or logically false — it might be perfectly understandable, just wrong or silly. Gibberish is specifically about incomprehensibility, not just being wrong.
  • Babble suggests continuous, fast, meaningless chatter — it emphasizes the flow of speech, whereas gibberish focuses more on the lack of meaning.
  • Jargon refers to specialized language of a particular field. Jargon becomes gibberish only to those who don't know the field — but to insiders, it is perfectly clear and meaningful.

Gibberish is any speech or writing that cannot be understood because it is either completely meaningless (made-up sounds, scrambled text, randomly combined words) or so impenetrably complex or corrupted that it might as well be meaningless. It is always uncountable as a noun, always carries a negative sense of "failure to communicate," and can arise by accident or on purpose.
